item.title: Leading Today, Building for Tomorrow - Special address by Shri Swaminathan J, Deputy Governor at the Leadership Conference of Indian Bank in Chennai on October 23, 2026 -
item.description:
Shri Binod Kumar, Managing Director and CEO; Executive Directors; senior colleagues from Indian Bank; ladies and gentlemen. Good morning. It is indeed a pleasure to be here with the senior leadership team of Indian Bank at your conference aptly themed ‘Leading through Emerging Challenges in Banking’.

2. One of the interesting paradoxes of leadership is that some of the most consequential decisions a leader makes may bear fruit long after his or her tenure has ended. Investments in technology, developing people, strengthening institutional capabilities, or even decisions about the direction in which an organisation should grow—these may take years to deliver their full benefits.

3. This is particularly relevant in banking, where institutions have a life and a responsibility that extend well beyond the tenure of any individual leader. A bank's strategy, culture and capabilities are shaped by successive generations of leadership, each building on the foundations laid by those who came before.

4. Indian Bank's own history illustrates this continuity. Established during the Swadeshi movement, the Bank commenced business on 15 August 1907, exactly forty years before India attained independence. From these origins, it has grown into a major public sector bank, carrying forward a legacy of service that now also encompasses the long banking tradition of the erstwhile Allahabad Bank.

5. The Bank's history also offers an instructive example of leadership in times of challenge. Many of you would be familiar with the turnaround of Indian Bank under the leadership of Smt. Ranjana Kumar1 in the early 2000s. It was an achievement that involved not merely financial restructuring, but also rebuilding confidence, strengthening organisational processes and mobilising the collective efforts of employees. The benefits of that transformation extended well beyond the tenure of the leadership that initiated it.

6. The institution that you lead today is thus the product of decisions and contributions made by generations of bankers before you. This raises an important question: How do we ensure that the decisions we take today not only deliver results during our tenure, but also leave the institution stronger and better prepared for the future?

7. This question has acquired particular significance in today's environment. The pace of technological change is accelerating, financial intermediation is evolving, economies and financial markets are becoming increasingly interconnected, and the expectations of customers have evolved significantly.

8. For bank leaders like yourselves, the challenge is therefore twofold. First, to deliver on the responsibilities of the present. Secondly, and more importantly, building the capabilities that will enable institutions to navigate an uncertain and changing future.

Understanding the changing landscape

9. The fundamental principles of banking have remained remarkably consistent over time. Banks must mobilise savings, allocate credit prudently, manage risks effectively and, above all, retain the confidence of their customers. These responsibilities are as relevant today as they were decades ago.

10. What instead has changed is the environment in which these responsibilities must be discharged, as mentioned before. Moreover, developments that once unfolded over several years can now reshape business models and competitive dynamics within a much shorter timeframe..

11. Three developments illustrate this changing landscape.

12. First, technology is transforming banking and reshaping customer expectations. Digital payments, artificial intelligence and advances in data analytics are changing how financial services are delivered. Customers increasingly expect banking to be convenient, seamless and available on demand. Their experiences with digital platforms in other sectors are also influencing what they expect from banks. For banks, the challenge is not merely to adopt new technologies, but to harness them to improve customer experience, operational efficiency and institutional competitiveness.

13. Secondly, the structure of financial intermediation is evolving. Banks now operate within a wider ecosystem of financial institutions, fintech companies, technology platforms and other service providers. This creates new opportunities for collaboration and innovation, while also changing competitive dynamics. At the same time, evolving household savings preferences and greater choices among financial products are changing the environment for deposit mobilisation. These developments call for renewed attention to business models, customer relationships and the strength of the deposit franchise.

14. Thirdly, the global economic and financial environment has become increasingly interconnected. Geopolitical developments, shifts in international trade and investment, and changes in global financial conditions can influence domestic economic activity through multiple channels. The growing linkages between financial markets, institutions and economies make it important for banks to look beyond their immediate operating environment. For leadership teams, this calls for a broader strategic perspective, an understanding of how external developments may affect their businesses, and the flexibility to respond to changing circumstances.

Building Institutions that endure

15. The developments I have outlined present banks with both opportunities and challenges. Responding effectively requires more than adjustments to business strategies or the adoption of new technologies. It calls for sustained investment in the capabilities that enable institutions to remain strong, competitive and trusted over time.

16. The Indian banking system approaches this task from a position of strength. Improvements in asset quality, capital adequacy and profitability over recent years have created a sound foundation for future growth. The important task now is to build on these gains and ensure that institutional capabilities keep pace with a changing environment.

17. In this context, I would emphasise a few key priorities.

Sustainable growth must remain at the heart of banking strategy.

18. Firstly, growth remains essential to the banking sector's role in supporting India's economic development. However, its sustainability depends on sound underwriting, appropriate risk pricing, and a clear understanding of borrowers' repayment capacity. Equally important is the liability side of the balance sheet. A stable and diversified deposit franchise supports sustainable credit expansion and reflects the depth of customer relationships. The objective should be to pursue growth that is balanced, appropriately funded and consistent with long-term institutional strength.

Operational and technological resilience has become far more relevant and is as important as credit or market risk.

19. Secondly, as banking becomes more digital, the reliability of technology infrastructure assumes increasing importance. Cybersecurity, data protection, business continuity and effective oversight of third-party service providers must be integral to institutional planning. These responsibilities extend beyond technology departments and require engagement across business functions and senior management. The objective is not simply to introduce new digital capabilities, but to ensure banking services remain dependable as operations scale and grow in complexity.

Sound governance and customer trust provide the foundations for enduring institutional strength.

20. Finally, governance must be reflected not only in policies and procedures, but also in the quality of decisions taken throughout the institution. Clear accountability, effective internal controls, transparency and a willingness to identify and address emerging issues are essential. Responsible lending, fair customer treatment, and effective grievance redressal remain central to public confidence. Ultimately, an institution's reputation is built on how consistently it fulfils its responsibilities to customers and other stakeholders.

Leading with foresight and purpose

21. Building institutions that endure ultimately comes down to leadership. Policies, systems and strategies provide the framework, but it is the judgement of leaders, the priorities they establish and the culture they foster that determine how effectively these translate into outcomes.

22. An important aspect of this stewardship is the willingness to look beyond immediate performance. Business targets and financial results are necessary measures of progress, but they cannot fully capture an institution's preparedness for the future.

23. Good leadership also requires the willingness to be challenged. Experience and institutional knowledge are invaluable in banking, but they must be complemented by an openness to new perspectives and a readiness to question established assumptions.

24. Leaders who encourage informed debate and welcome differing viewpoints create an environment in which better decisions can emerge, and potential problems can be identified early.

25. A lasting institution requires leadership at every level, not just at the top. One of the most valuable contributions of senior management is to identify talent, entrust people with responsibility and prepare them to exercise independent judgement. This involves more than formal succession planning. It requires creating opportunities for younger colleagues to take initiative, learn from experience and develop the confidence to lead.

26. Leadership also involves knowing what to preserve and what to change. Established values, institutional experience and sound banking principles provide continuity. Business practices, organisational structures and ways of working, however, must remain open to review as circumstances evolve. The challenge is neither to preserve everything that is familiar nor to embrace every new idea, but to exercise sound judgement in distinguishing between the two.

27. In the final analysis, the legacy of leadership extends beyond business achievements or individual milestones. It lies in the quality of the institution handed over to those who follow — its people, its systems, its values and its capacity to meet future challenges. A leader's most enduring achievement may well be an institution that continues to grow stronger long after the leader has moved on.

Conclusion

28. As I conclude, I am reminded of the words of former President Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam when he inaugurated Indian Bank's centenary celebrations in September 2006. Reflecting on the qualities of creative leadership, he spoke of the need to change the traditional role “from commander to coach, manager to mentor, from director to delegator and from one who demands respect to one who facilitates self-respect.”2

29. These words, addressed to an earlier generation of Indian Bank's leadership, remain relevant even today. They remind us that effective leadership is not simply about exercising authority or achieving business targets. It is about empowering people, nurturing their abilities, and creating an environment where they can contribute their best to the institution.

30. The opportunities before Indian banking are considerable, as are the responsibilities that accompany them. Realising these opportunities will require institutions to remain open to innovation while maintaining their commitment to prudence, sound governance and customer trust.

31. In an environment of continuous change, the most successful banking institutions will be those that combine the confidence to innovate, the discipline to remain resilient, and the foresight to prepare for the future.

32. I am confident that Indian Bank will continue to draw upon its institutional strengths and the commitment of its leadership team to contribute meaningfully to India's economic progress.

33. My best wishes to all of you for productive and fruitful discussions during the Conference. Thank you. Jai Hind.

1 Smt. Ranjana Kumar served as Chairman and Managing Director of Indian Bank from May 2000 to November 2003, the first woman to head a public sector bank and is often credited with leading one of the most significant performance turnarounds in Indian banking history. With negative capital adequacy and six consecutive years of losses, the bank turned around successfully, meeting all targets under the restructuring plan, and returning to net profits. She later served as Chairperson of NABARD (2003-2005) and as a Vigilance Commissioner in the Central Vigilance Commission.

2 Kalam, A. P. J. Abdul (2006), “Banking for Rural Prosperity”, address at the inauguration of the centenary celebrations of Indian Bank, Chennai. Available at: https://presidentofindia.nic.in/dr-apj-abdul-kalam/speeches/address-inauguration-centenary-celebrations-indian-bankchennai (last accessed on October 20, 2026)

item.title: Economic Resilience, Thinner Buffers, Emerging Risks Globally: Where Does India Stand?<sup>[1]</sup> - Address by Dr. Poonam Gupta, Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India, at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit -
item.description:
It is a pleasure to be back at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit. When I spoke here last year, my theme was the macroeconomic resilience of emerging markets (EMs), including India, which I attributed to the sound policy frameworks that these economies have adopted and adhered to.

A year on, the resilience of the world economy has held. In today’s talk, I will reflect on the latest global outlook drawing on the recent publications of the IMF, how India is placed in this global context, and what policy priorities may be warranted for other EMs as well as India at this point in time.

My observations are in four parts, one each on growth, inflation, public finances and the financial sector.

1. Growth rates seem resilient across countries

The IMF’s latest World Economic Outlook (WEO, October 2026) projects the global economy to grow at 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027. The projection for 2026 is 0.1 percentage point higher than in July, and that for 2027 is unchanged. While these numbers are below the pre-pandemic (2000–19) average of 3.7 per cent and the 2022–25 average of 3.5 per cent, they show continued resilience, given the underlying challenges the global economy has been facing.2 In fact, actual growth has turned out stronger than projected by the IMF in each of the past three years, even as shocks have accumulated and intensified.

A few more features of the latest projection deserve attention. First, the latest upgrade is accounted for by advanced economies (AEs), whose growth projection for 2026 has been raised by 0.4 percentage point to 2.1 per cent. More than half of this upgrade for AEs comes from the group of “other AEs”, which includes technology exporters such as Korea, and whose projection has been raised by 1.4 percentage points, along with smaller upgrades in Europe, including Germany (0.6 percentage point). The projection for the United States is unchanged at 2.3 per cent.3 Second, the projection for emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) has been marginally lowered by 0.1 percentage point to 3.7 per cent (Chart 1).4 Third, the projection for India in 2026-27 has been upgraded by 0.6 percentage point to 7.0 per cent.

What explains this resilience? WEO attributes it to “a combination of circumstantial and institutional factors as well as offsetting forces”.

The first set is circumstantial, starting with the financial cushions that households and firms built up in earlier years. The large fiscal support during the pandemic cushioned their finances, and many had shifted to longer-term borrowing at fixed rates while interest rates were low, which has shielded them from the recent rise in rates. In 2025, financial conditions were accommodative and fiscal stimulus also supported activity.

The second is institutional: better policy frameworks. Central banks have earned credibility, which has kept inflation expectations in check, and frameworks for monetary, fiscal and financial policy have improved. In emerging markets in particular, central banks have become more independent, monetary policy is better implemented, and exchange rates are more flexible and better able to absorb shocks. According to the IMF, these improvements explain slightly more than half of the better output performance of emerging markets during global risk-off episodes, with favourable external conditions explaining the rest.

The third is a set of offsetting forces and the ability to adapt. Tariffs turned out lower than first announced, firms found ways around trade barriers, investment in artificial intelligence (AI) picked up, and oil producers outside the Gulf raised output while inventories were released. Besides, the energy used per dollar of world GDP has fallen by about a third over the past two decades. All this has reduced the impact of the near closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The IMF estimates that the closure will take 0.3 percentage point off global growth in 2026, against 0.9 percentage point had oil supply been less flexible and energy use less efficient.5

Investment in AI has also supported growth. Large investments in data centres and computing equipment have boosted demand, well ahead of any visible gains in productivity. According to a recent IMF blog, AI could add about half a percentage point to annual world growth over the next decade.6 These gains, however, may take time and are likely to be unevenly distributed across countries.

The risks to the outlook are seen as tilted to the downside. These include a prolonged or wider conflict in West Asia and Ukraine, which would push commodity prices higher; a reassessment of the expected gains from AI, whose supply chain is highly concentrated; extreme weather, made worse by El Niño; rising long-term borrowing costs in the major AEs; and renewed trade tensions. It also cautions that “the margins of adjustment are narrowing”, that the resilience so far has relied on governments drawing on their fiscal space, and that in most countries this space now needs to be rebuilt.

While upgrading India, WEO has projected growth of 7.0 per cent in both 2026-27 and 2027-28, the highest among the 21 economies whose GDP exceeded US$1 trillion in 2025 (Chart 2). Looking further ahead, it notes that “India stands out with upward revisions, reflecting sustained momentum and growing evidence of stronger growth potential supported by favourable demographic dynamics, a large and expanding domestic market, and continued structural reforms.”

Defying multiple odds, the Indian economy grew by 7.8 per cent in 2025-26. Dynamism is on display this year too, when growth in the first quarter of 2026-27 (April–June 2026), after the conflict in West Asia broke out, was registered at 7.8 per cent, and was higher than expected. Growth was driven mainly by private consumption and fixed investment, with the latter growing by 11.9 per cent, its highest in the new GDP series.7 Exports of goods and services grew by 12.0 per cent in real terms, as merchandise exports picked up and services exports stayed strong. On the supply side, manufacturing grew by 9.2 per cent and services by 9.7 per cent. Growth is not just high but balanced as well.

The economic momentum seems to have carried into July–September. Gross goods and services tax (GST) collections rose by more than 14 per cent in each month of the quarter. Industrial output was up 8.0 per cent in August. Merchandise exports have grown at double-digit rates for six months running, by 23.0 per cent in September. Both the manufacturing and the services Purchasing Managers’ Indices (PMIs) were above 55 in September. Bank credit grew by 19.4 per cent year on year as on September 30, and retail automobile sales rose by 31.8 per cent in September, with two-wheeler sales up 33.1 per cent (partly because purchases had been deferred a year earlier ahead of the GST rate cuts).8

At this point, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) expects growth of 7.1 per cent in 2026-27, 0.4 percentage point more than what was projected in August.

What explains India’s ability to stand out? It is not that India has faced fewer shocks. In fact, over the past year and a half, India has been subjected to almost all the recent shocks at the same time: among the highest tariffs imposed by the US on any trading partner; an oil price shock, as a large net importer of oil; El Niño and a deficient monsoon; and capital outflows, as global investors favoured AI-related assets in other markets. Yet the economy has withstood them well. In my view, it is not due to good luck; four factors explain this.

First, India is a large and diversified economy, with a vast domestic market. Its growth is spatially broad-based, diversified and underpinned by rising productivity, and it draws on domestic consumption as well as exports.9 As a result, even when particular sectors are hit by specific shocks, large parts of the economy remain relatively insulated. This stands in contrast to economies that rely on a narrower set of growth drivers, such as natural resources, agriculture, external demand rather than domestic markets, or remittances from outward migration, or that face unfavourable demographics.

Second, India’s policy frameworks have improved, and so has their implementation, with a firm focus on macroeconomic and financial stability. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management framework has anchored fiscal consolidation within a rules-based path; GST has unified the indirect tax system; flexible inflation targeting, adopted in 2016, has lowered both the level and the volatility of inflation; and banking regulation and supervision have been considerably strengthened.

Third, due to conscious policy actions, the economy has become less sensitive to some of the shocks that used to hurt it in the past. Agricultural growth is less affected by deficient or erratic rainfall, owing to crop diversification, expanded irrigation and more accurate weather information. The economy now uses less oil for each unit of output, so that changes in oil prices have a smaller impact on the current account and on growth.

Fourth is the manner in which the shocks have been managed: with policy certainty, deeper engagement with stakeholders, clearer communication and timely action. When the energy shock struck, the priority was to secure adequate supplies rather than pass the shock on to consumers, and rationing was largely avoided; higher prices were passed on gradually, once it became clear that they would remain elevated. Trade partners have been diversified, free trade agreements fast-tracked and diplomatic channels used, while the rationalisation of GST has supported consumption. At the same time, there was no attempt to stimulate demand beyond the economy’s productive capacity, and fiscal consolidation has stayed on track.10

2. Higher inflation across countries, resulting in tighter monetary policy

WEO projects global headline inflation at 4.7 per cent in 2026, up from 4.1 per cent in 2025, and expects it to ease back to 4.1 per cent in 2027. Inflation in 2026 is projected to be above its pre-pandemic (2000–19) average of 3.9 per cent, though below the 2022–25 average of 6.3 per cent.

Three factors are shaping the inflation outlook. The first is the re-escalation of the conflict in West Asia, which has pushed up the prices of energy and other commodities. The IMF now expects oil prices to average about US$96 a barrel in 2026, 16 per cent higher than it had assumed in April, and fertiliser prices to rise by 10 per cent. Higher costs of energy, fertilisers, transport and insurance are, in turn, projected to raise international food prices by 5 per cent.

The second is El Niño which typically puts upward pressure on food and commodity prices. It also weighs on activity, especially in economies where food has a large weight in the consumption basket. Food prices have already been rising: the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Food Price Index rose by 4.5 per cent during June–September, mainly because of transport disruptions and weather concerns.

The third is the boom in AI-related investment. Large spending on data centres, chips and power infrastructure is a sizeable addition to demand, concentrated in a few economies, and in some sectors supply has not kept pace with it. So far, the effects on core inflation in the major economies appear limited, but where economies are already running close to capacity, prices could rise more widely.

The first two are supply shocks, while the third is a demand impulse that is unevenly spread across countries. How much each country is affected depends on how much it relies on imported energy, the weight of food in its consumption basket, and the strength of its domestic demand.

In AEs, in particular, inflation has been above their target in every year since 2022 (Chart 3).11 The IMF projects it at 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 2.7 per cent in 2027, returning close to 2 per cent only from 2028. In EMDEs too, inflation, at 5.7 per cent in 2026, is projected to be at the upper end of the 3–6 per cent range of their targets.

For India, the IMF projects inflation to rise from 2.0 per cent in 2025-26 to 5.0 per cent in 2026-27, before moderating to 4.4 per cent in 2027-28.

The current situation of external shocks and the resultant growth–inflation outlook raises the following questions about how countries may conduct their monetary policy.

How should monetary policy respond to supply shocks, and distinguish temporary external price shocks from more persistent second-round effects? Are inflation-targeting frameworks adequately equipped to deal with repeated supply shocks? If not, how should they evolve as the frequency and nature of global shocks change? What role should communication play during periods of uncertainty? How should fiscal and monetary policy coordinate in managing external supply shocks? How may AI further change the macroeconomic environment, and therefore the monetary policy frameworks and policy choices? Finally, how may central banks in emerging economies navigate narrowing interest-rate differentials with AEs, given their implications for exchange rates, capital flows and monetary policy autonomy?

Central banks generally look through the direct impact of temporary supply shocks but watch closely for signs of price pressures spreading across the economy. To do so, they strengthen their analytical tools and surveys. They distinguish between generalisation through input cost pressures and more persistent second-round effects through wages and expectations. For this, they track a range of indicators, including diffusion indices that measure the breadth of price pressures, the trajectory of wages, and inflation expectations.

At the same time, policy makers may not always have the luxury of waiting for these effects to fully materialise and may instead take pre-emptive actions. The IMF has emphasised that monetary policy “should remain firmly focused on price stability”, with a policy stance restrictive enough to bring inflation back to target in a timely manner and prevent second-round effects.12

The flexibility built into inflation-targeting frameworks, including the tolerance band or an explicit or implicit mandate of growth or employment, has helped central banks adapt their response to the specific challenges and contexts. Central banks are communicating more and better. This has helped anchor expectations and preserve credibility despite not meeting the inflation targets for multiple years. The question, however, remains whether they can continue to anchor expectations for a much longer period without actually meeting their targets, as is the case currently for many AEs.

One direct implication is that monetary policy may not have enough room to respond if current shocks persist or new shocks emerge, especially when countries have consistently breached their respective targets. The IMF makes a related point. Monetary policy can look through supply shocks only if they are temporary and second-round effects remain contained, and these conditions “are less likely to be satisfied when inflation is already above target and broader price pressures are expected to remain elevated, justifying a bias toward tightening”.

Fiscal policy, together with closer coordination between monetary and fiscal authorities, also has a role to play in the current circumstances. As in India and elsewhere, it can help cushion the initial impact of supply shocks, through targeted supply-side measures. Such interventions, however, must be consistent with continued fiscal prudence and overall macroeconomic stability.

As for AI, its overall implications for inflation and monetary policy are still being assessed. In the near term, the investment boom adds to demand, as noted earlier. Once AI raises productivity, it could lower costs and ease inflation, although inflation could pick up again later if higher demand comes to dominate. If it lifts investment demand and expected growth for a sustained period, it could also raise the neutral interest rate. And wider use of AI in pricing could allow firms to adjust prices more quickly, so that shocks pass through to inflation faster than in the past.13

Central banks in emerging economies are generally guided by domestic growth and inflation conditions, and the specific monetary policy frameworks or inflation-targeting frameworks that they have put in place rather than by interest-rate differentials with AEs. There are hardly any central banks that incorporate external conditions or the exchange rate directly into their inflation-targeting mandate.14 Most others factor external spillovers, financial market volatility and exchange rate developments into monetary policy decisions only to the extent that they transmit into domestic inflation or financial stability.

Price pressures have built up in India from very benign levels in 2025-26. Headline CPI inflation increased to 4.8 per cent in August from 4.5 per cent in July. While the increase was mainly on account of food and fuel, core inflation also rose, to 4.2 per cent, indicating some widening of price pressures.15 In October, the MPC raised the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent.

As Governor noted in his statement, “Inflationary pressures are, however, building up”, and therefore it was considered “appropriate to recalibrate the policy rate”. The stance was changed to calibrated tightening, “essentially signalling that rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving circumstances and the outlook”.16 Inflation data for September, released after the policy meeting, were along expected lines: headline inflation rose to 5.5 per cent and core inflation to 4.3 per cent, so that the average for July–September, at 4.9 per cent, was the same as the MPC’s projection for the quarter.

Over a longer period, India’s record on inflation has been rather strong. Since the adoption of flexible inflation targeting in 2016, annual inflation has declined from the previous years’ average, has become more stable, and has remained within the tolerance band of 2 to 6 per cent in all but two years (Chart 4). Even in those two years of exceptional external circumstances (Covid and the Russia–Ukraine war), it did not deviate too much from the upper limit, at 6.2 and 6.7 per cent, and declined subsequently.

3. Thinner buffers globally, especially fiscal, to respond to the current shock if it persists, or to address a new shock

The fiscal situation of most countries seems to be stretched. Public spending rose sharply during the pandemic and the shocks that followed, and it has proven hard for most countries to rebuild their fiscal buffers.

Of the 190 economies with data for both years in the IMF’s Fiscal Monitor database, 119 had a higher debt ratio in 2025 than in 2019. Global public debt was 94 per cent of GDP in 2025. It is projected to cross 100 per cent in 2030 and to reach close to 102 per cent in 2031. Debt ratios are projected to rise in both AEs and EMDEs, from 108 and 74 per cent of GDP, respectively, in 2025 to 115 and 84 per cent in 2031 (Chart 5). Higher debt leaves governments less room to respond to a new shock, particularly when interest costs are rising.

Borrowing costs have also risen, which makes high debt harder to service. Ten-year sovereign bond yields in the G7 increased, on average, by more than one percentage point between February and September 2026, to their highest levels in almost twenty years. This reflects several factors: the oil price shock, inflation that has proved persistent, stronger demand for investment, and expectations of faster growth from AI. Concerns about public finances have added to the pressure, given high debt, rising spending needs and the prospect of heavy bond issuance.17

This brings us to the question of debt sustainability. Whether the debt ratios across countries rise or fall depends on two things: the primary deficit (non-interest expenditure in excess of revenue), and the gap between the interest rate a government pays on its debt and the growth rate of nominal GDP.

For the median advanced and emerging market economies, this gap was negative in every year from 2016 to 2025, except 2020. While remaining negative, it is projected to narrow over the next few years (Chart 6). As the gap narrows, governments will need to run smaller primary deficits to stabilise their debt ratios. Instead, the primary deficit is projected to rise from 2.5 to 3.0 per cent of GDP in AEs, and to fall only marginally, from 3.9 to 3.8 per cent, in emerging market economies. In each case, it will exceed the primary deficit that would stabilise the debt ratio.

India’s projected debt path is different, and much more benign. General-government debt is projected to decline from 84.3 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 75.1 per cent by 2031-32. Nominal GDP growth, at about 11 per cent a year, is projected to stay well above the effective interest rate of about 7 per cent, leaving a gap of around -4 percentage points through 2031-32 (Chart 6). India’s primary deficit has also been much smaller than the global averages. The debt ratio therefore declines even though the primary deficit stays between 1.7 and 2.2 per cent of GDP.18

The IMF makes the same point about the largest advanced and emerging market economies: “In most of these economies, with India an exception, stabilising debt-to-GDP ratios at 2025 levels would require greater fiscal consolidation than currently envisaged under existing policies.” Indeed, among the nine emerging market economies with GDP above US$1 trillion, India is the only one whose debt ratio is projected to decline between 2025 and 2031.19

So how sustainable is India’s public debt? Sustainability can be assessed in different ways. One could assess the rollover risk, that is, whether the government may find it difficult or costly to refinance its maturing debt. Another is runaway risk, that is, whether the debt ratio may keep rising on its own momentum, because the interest rate on debt exceeds the growth rate of the economy. India has neither. Most of the public debt is long term, is denominated in local currency, and is held domestically (a large part of which is held by institutional investors), which limits rollover risk. And a favourable growth and interest-rate differential, along with fiscal consolidation, has put the debt ratio on a declining path.

Fiscal consolidation has also been accompanied by more fiscal transparency and an improvement in the quality of expenditure. Capital expenditure of the general government has risen from about 13 per cent of total expenditure in 2020-21 to nearly 20 per cent in 2025-26 (budget estimates), and from about 4 per cent of GDP in 2019-20 to 5.8 per cent in 2025-26.20 Higher capital expenditure can itself help make debt sustainable by crowding in private investment and raising the economy’s growth and growth potential.

India has not relied exclusively on fiscal measures to respond to shocks. An “all of system” approach has been used to manage the fallout of the shocks rather than resorting to fiscal measures as the first or only line of defense. The endeavour has been to remain fiscally prudent and fiscally sustainable.

The IMF advises that rebuilding fiscal space is now urgent, given high debt and higher borrowing costs. It calculates that reforms addressing existing fiscal distortions together could lift GDP by several per cent over time.

4. Financial sector has held up well globally, but could face shocks

With the changing global order and rapid transformation of the financial systems, safeguarding financial stability has become an ever more compelling priority. The Global Financial Crisis (GFC) of 2007–09 showed that financial instability can cost dearly in terms of economic growth, fiscal backstop, and rebuilding trust. The reforms that followed have strengthened bank regulation, supervision and risk management, and the capacity of banks to absorb shocks. As a result, the banking sector has become much more resilient. For the largest internationally active banks, the average common equity Tier 1 capital ratio nearly doubled, from 7.1 per cent in June 2011 to 13.3 per cent at the end of 2021. According to the Basel Committee’s evaluation, systemic risk declined after the reforms, with no considerable evidence of adverse effects on bank lending.21

The post-GFC reforms have strengthened the global financial system’s ability to withstand recurring shocks and periods of uncertainty, but the resilience also rested on exceptional monetary and fiscal support, and the rapidity of policy response. This helps explain why episodes such as the 2020 ‘dash for cash’, the UK’s 2022 liability-driven investment crisis and the sporadic 2023 events in US and European banks were contained promptly before they created wider repercussions.

The question is whether this resilience will hold up against the shocks that lie ahead, which are likely to be different from those of the past. They may come from outside the financial system, such as geopolitics, AI, cyber attacks or climate events, rather than from a domestic credit boom. They may also originate in non-banks, markets and technology providers rather than in banks, spread faster, and affect several parts of the system at once.

In addition, the latest edition of the IMF’s Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR) has identified three topical risks: a fall in the prices of AI-related assets, if investment and profits in AI prove weaker or less durable than expected; a sharp increase in sovereign bond yields, from renewed inflation or concerns about public finances; and cyber threats, which are becoming a systemic risk as financial services grow more digital and interconnected.

GFSR notes, these “could be near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”. Their impact could be amplified by leverage, concentrated exposures and liquidity mismatches, particularly among non-bank financial institutions. This could test the resilience of the global financial system at a time when policy space is narrowing. The overall assessment is that while financial markets have been resilient, risks to financial stability remain elevated.22

The GFSR therefore calls for containing excessive leverage, bringing public debt onto a sustainable path, preserving the capital and liquidity buffers of banks, improving data to assess risks across the system, putting credible backstops in place, and, in emerging markets, rebuilding fiscal and external buffers.

How well placed is India to deal with these risks? On at least two of these three risks, India is better placed: its markets are not exhibiting a bubble-like situation, related to AI or otherwise; and its fiscal house is in order. As for cyber risks, it is working in line with global best practices.

India also had its own cycle of vulnerabilities, to which policy responded swiftly, although it may not seem too well aligned with the global cycle mentioned above.

Following a prolonged credit boom in the 2000s, India faced a twin balance-sheet problem involving banks and corporates in the 2010s, and institution-specific events in 2018–23. These challenges prompted reforms on three fronts: recognition of bad loans, through the Asset Quality Review; their resolution, through the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code; and regulation, through a revised Prompt Corrective Action framework and scale-based regulation of non-banking financial companies (NBFCs).23 Countercyclical measures were undertaken too, as warranted (e.g. in November 2023, when regulatory measures on consumer credit and bank credit to NBFCs were implemented).

The resilience of the Indian financial system is now amply evident: capital adequacy is 17.7 per cent, the common equity Tier 1 ratio is 15.3 per cent, and the liquidity coverage ratio is about 124 per cent. The gross non-performing asset (NPA) ratio of scheduled commercial banks has declined from 11.6 per cent in March 2018 to 1.8 per cent in March 2026, a multi-decadal low.

RBI’s stress tests reinforce this assessment. The June 2026 Financial Stability Report included adverse scenarios built around a prolonged and wider geopolitical conflict. Even under the most severe scenario, the capital adequacy of the 46 major banks would remain at about 13 per cent by March 2028, well above the regulatory minimum of 9 per cent, while the gross NPA ratio would rise from 1.8 per cent to about 4 per cent.24

India has achieved strong compliance ratings under the Basel Committee’s Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme for key elements of the Basel III framework, including risk-based capital requirements, the net stable funding ratio and the large-exposures framework, with the liquidity coverage ratio assessed as largely compliant.25 The Financial Stability Report has been a key instrument for assessing the resilience of our financial system. Over 16 years and 33 half-yearly editions, it has become a core part of our macroprudential toolkit. It helps us identify and communicate vulnerabilities, and test how the financial system would cope with shocks. It has also become more forward-looking over time, with better stress tests, a system-wide stress indicator, stability maps and thematic surveys.

Preserving financial stability is a shared responsibility that extends beyond the central bank and requires coordinated action by all financial regulators and the government. India’s inter-agency framework serves this purpose. The Financial Stability and Development Council, chaired by the Finance Minister, and its Sub-Committee, chaired by the RBI Governor, provide an institutional platform for the government, the RBI and all financial sector regulators to exchange information, assess systemic risks and coordinate policy responses to safeguard financial stability.

India’s financial resilience thus rests on several factors: healthy balance sheets, a strong regulatory framework that balances risk management with economic growth, supervision that is risk-based and makes good use of technology, countercyclical policies to prevent vulnerabilities from building up during periods of rapid growth, a broad regulatory perimeter that helps limit regulatory arbitrage, stress tests to assess the vulnerability to envisaged shocks, and all-encompassing forums to discuss such risks.26

5. Concluding thoughts

The global economy has been resilient so far, but three risks could test this resilience. The first is energy security, with oil prices at around US$100 a barrel, and at times higher, while fuel and gas supplies from the Gulf remain disrupted. Besides the price of oil, shipping and insurance costs have risen manifold, and this is being reflected in the prices of other commodities too. High prices are likely to persist into 2027, while El Niño poses a risk to food security.

The second is AI. It is proving to be an engine of global growth, through an investment boom, and holds productivity potential for years to come. But the investment is increasingly debt-financed and concentrated in a few firms and countries. Whether it is a bubble, and whether it will deflate, only time will tell. But it has reached a stage where even slight news or minor events can result in significant price reactions.

The third is public debt and borrowing costs. Global public debt is heading above 100 per cent of GDP, bond yields have risen sharply, and EMDEs face costlier funding and more volatile capital flows.

Let me bring these threads together for India. On growth, India stands out. It is the fastest-growing large economy, and unlike the EMDE aggregate, its growth projection has been revised up over the past year. That growth has rested more on domestic sources lately, particularly private consumption and public investment, but new drivers have emerged, including private investment and merchandise exports. The ballpark estimate that most agencies have for the next few years is 7 per cent or thereabouts. With some of the conditions normalising, and with continued policy attention, one could envisage growth moving up from 7 per cent towards 8 per cent.

India’s track record on inflation over the last ten years has been equally credible. Since the adoption of flexible inflation targeting, inflation has declined structurally, has remained within the tolerance band in most years, and has become less volatile. The MPC and the RBI remain committed to the inflation-targeting framework.

On public finances, India has stayed on the path of fiscal consolidation, even as deficits and debt have risen in many other countries. Its general-government debt is projected to decline by about 9 percentage points of GDP by 2031-32, and it faces neither rollover risk nor runaway risk.

India’s financial sector is on a strong footing. Banks’ capital adequacy is at 17.7 per cent and the gross NPA ratio at a multi-decadal low of 1.8 per cent, and stress tests show that banks would remain well capitalised even under severe scenarios. We nevertheless remain watchful of spillovers from global financial markets, as well as of cyber and climate risks.

All in all, the global economy has been resilient, but its buffers have thinned. India enters this phase in a stronger position than most: growth is strong, inflation is contained, public debt is on a declining path and the financial system is sound.

item.title: Growth with Responsibility: The Next Balance Sheet - Special Address by Shri Swaminathan J, Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India at the FE Modern BFSI Summit 2026 in Mumbai on October 15, 2026 -
item.description:
Shri Tuhin Kanta Pandey, Chairman, SEBI; Shri Shyamal Majumdar, Editor, and friends from the Financial Express, distinguished leaders from banking, financial services and insurance; ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to all of you.

2. We meet as the festive season gathers momentum across the country— a period traditionally associated with celebration and elevated economic activity. Veterans amongst us here will recall that this was once known as the “busy season” for credit policy. For households and businesses, this is also a time when important financial decisions are often made, whether to spend or invest for the future, like purchase a home or expand an enterprise.

3. For the financial sector, this represents both opportunity and responsibility. Finance helps translate confidence into economic activity, but its ability to do so depends in turn on the confidence that customers place in financial institutions.

4. That makes the theme of today's Summit — “The Next Balance Sheet: Growth. Trust. Resilience.” — particularly relevant. The Indian financial system enters its next phase from a position of strength, with improved asset quality and comfortable capital positions. The challenge is to preserve these strengths as the system grows, becomes increasingly technology-intensive and ever more interconnected.

5. In this context, I would like to make three propositions:

(i) First, as institutions pursue growth and remove friction, controls must evolve with the process.

(ii) Second, trust must be treated as an asset that requires continuous investment.

(iii) And third, resilience must increasingly be understood not only in terms of buffers, but also in terms of the speed with which an institution can detect, decide and recover.

Growth with discipline of control

6. Several sessions today deal with frictionless onboarding, digital public infrastructure, AI-led underwriting and autonomous workflows. These developments can indeed reduce costs, improve customer experience and extend financial services to customers who were previously difficult to serve.

7. However, from a supervisory perspective, not every friction in finance is inefficiency. Some frictions perform an important control function. An independent verification, a maker-checker arrangement or a cooling-off period may add time to a process, but they can also reduce the probability of error, fraud or adverse selection.

8. Technology may allow some of these steps to be delayered, redesigned or automated, but before removing them an institution should understand the function they were performing. If a manual check is replaced by an algorithm, or underwriting becomes instantaneous, the underlying risk does not disappear; the control must therefore evolve with the process. In supervisory terms, the control environment must remain commensurate with the pace and nature of growth.

9. The same principle applies when activities are carried out through third parties. A loan may be sourced through a fintech, a product distributed through an external platform, or a decision supported by a third-party model. The process may be outsourced, but the responsibility associated with the institution’s licence remains with the regulated entity.

10. A practical question, therefore, is that whenever a step is removed or modified in the name of speed, scale or customer convenience, what risk was that step controlling, and where does that control now reside? If the answer is not clear, process simplification may in fact be control dilution.

Trust as an asset

11. My second proposition concerns trust. Financial institutions depend upon it, yet it does not appear explicitly on the balance sheet. We do not recognise trust when it is built, but when it is impaired the effects can become visible quickly through customer attrition, litigation, regulatory penalties, and reputational damage.

12. The invisible nature of trust makes it easy to underinvest in during good times. When growth is strong, customer acquisition is healthy and profitability is comfortable, the return from investing in conduct, service quality or grievance handling may appear less immediate. Yet these are often the areas where early signs of weakness first emerge.

13. One area wherein trust is tested is the sale of financial products. Technology allows institutions to understand customers better, reach them more frequently and tailor products with finer precision. These capabilities can improve customer outcomes, but they can also sharpen the consequences of poor incentive design. When the pressure to complete a transaction becomes stronger than the obligation to assess whether it serves the customer’s needs, trust can deteriorate even while business volumes are rising.

14. A second area is the use of customer data. As institutions gain the ability to personalise products and services in real time, the question is not only whether consent has been obtained, but whether the use of that data is consistent with what the customer would reasonably expect. The more powerful the analytical capability, the greater the need for discipline in how that capability is exercised.

15. A third area is grievance handling. Complaints should not be seen merely as service issues to be resolved and closed; they can be an important source of risk intelligence. A pattern of complaints may reveal weaknesses in product design, incentive structures, digital journeys or third-party arrangements. Institutions that learn from grievances, rather than simply dispose of them, are likely to identify emerging problems earlier.

16. Trust also has a system-wide dimension. A customer who loses money through fraud may not distinguish between the institution where the fraud originated, the institution through which the funds moved, and the institution that may have hosted a mule account. From the customer’s perspective, the financial system has failed. Weak controls in one part of the system can therefore impose a trust cost on the whole system.

Resilience in an age of compressed time

17. My third proposition concerns resilience. Capital, liquidity and provisioning remain fundamental, but in a more digital and intermeshed financial system, resilience must also be measured in time. The key questions are increasingly how quickly an institution can detect a problem, comprehend its implications, decide and restore critical services.

18. Technology has compressed the time in which risks can develop and propagate. The 2023 banking stress in the United States showed how sharply such timelines can compress: US$42 billion of deposits moving in a single day is not something that could have happened through a queue outside a bank branch.

19. In a more digital financial system, resilience therefore depends not only on the capacity to absorb a shock, but also on the speed with which an institution can detect, assess and respond to it.

20. This places a premium on the speed and quality of internal information flows. In many cases, significant problems are not wholly invisible before they become serious. An auditor may have identified an exception, a compliance officer may have raised a concern, or a business unit may already have observed an unusual pattern. The challenge is whether that information gets to those with the authority to act, and whether it does so in time.

21. One useful measure of governance quality, therefore, is the time it takes for bad news to travel through the institution. Where risk, compliance and audit functions have sufficient stature, escalation is encouraged and Boards actively seek out emerging concerns, institutions are better placed to respond before problems become difficult to contain.

Conclusion

22. As we think about the next balance sheet, the festive season offers a useful analogy. In one interpretation1, the nine days of Navratri are grouped into three triads — the first associated with Durga, the next with Lakshmi and the final with Saraswati.

23. The sequence is instructive: strength comes first, prosperity follows, and wisdom and discernment help sustain it. In financial terms, resilience provides the foundation for growth, while sound judgement and governance build the trust that allows that growth to endure.

24. A similar idea is reflected in the Diwali tradition of opening new account books and beginning them with the words ‘Shubh Labh’. The emphasis is not only on ‘Labh’ — gain or prosperity — but also on ‘Shubh’, that is, the quality and legitimacy of that gain are equally important.

25. For financial institutions, that is a useful test of the next balance sheet. Growth should not be judged only by its pace or scale, but also by the strength of the controls behind it, the fairness of the conduct that supports it, and the trust it is able to sustain.

26. As we move through this season of renewal and optimism, I wish the financial sector growth that is not only strong, but also sound, trusted and durable. The opportunities before us are considerable, but so too is the responsibility to ensure that innovation is matched by judgement, growth by sound controls, and ambition with resilience. If we can preserve that balance, the next balance sheet will not only be larger; it will also be stronger.

27. With this, I wish all of you a fruitful and successful summit. Thank you. Jai Hind.

1 Swami Tejomayananda, “The Spiritual Significance of Navaratri,” Chinmaya Mission, May 1, 2025, https://www.chinmayamission.com/global/article/the-spiritual-significance-of-navaratri-swami-tejomayananda

item.title: Edited Transcript of the Reserve Bank of India’s Post-Monetary Policy Press Conference: October 7, 2026 (Wednesday) -
item.description:
Participants from the Reserve Bank of India:
Shri Sanjay Malhotra - Governor, Reserve Bank of India
Shri Swaminathan J - Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India
Dr. Poonam Gupta - Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India
Shri Shirish Chandra Murmu - Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India
Shri Rohit Jain - Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India
Shri Sanjay Kumar Hansda - Executive Director, Reserve Bank of India
Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya - Executive Director, Reserve Bank of India
Shri Ravi Shankar - Executive Director, Reserve Bank of India

Moderator:
Shri Brij Raj - Chief General Manager, Reserve Bank of India

Brij Raj:
Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to this post-policy press conference, fourth for the financial year 2026-27. We have with us Governor, Reserve Bank of India, Shri Sanjay Malhotra; along with Deputy Governors, Shri Swaminathan J; Dr. Poonam Gupta; Shri Shirish Chandra Murmu; and Shri Rohit Jain. We also have with us Executive Directors, Shri Sanjay Kumar Hansda; Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya; and Shri Ravi Shankar. I also welcome my other colleagues from the Reserve Bank.

Sir, there are 26 participants from the media. Before we begin, we have two housekeeping announcements. First, I request the media participants to please stick to only one question. I repeat, one question only, so that everyone gets a chance. Second, please switch on the mic while speaking so that those watching the live telecast are able to hear clearly. Once you have finished speaking, please switch off the mic.

Sir, with your permission, I will now call out the names.

Sanjay Malhotra:
Yes, let's begin.

Brij Raj:
Thank you, Sir. I will request Ms. Latha Venkatesh from CNBC TV18 to please ask the first question. Latha, please.

Latha Venkatesh, CNBC TV18:
Thank you very much. Thank you Governor and RBI. Sir, you in your speech, pointed out that the next three quarters, the inflation average is 5.8%. Now, that means it is still a very loose policy in terms of real rate. Did you all contemplate a 50-basis hike at all? Going by the minutes of the previous MPC meeting, you said that you will recalibrate policy as inflation normalizes. Should we expect the recalibration of real rate also in the policies to come?

Sanjay Malhotra:
So, there are two parts to the same question, right? One is that did you consider a 50-basis point rate hike? So, we discuss all possibilities and thereafter take a view as to what will be the appropriate monetary policy decision.

As regard to the real rate, obviously, a recalibration thereof, even a 25-basis points hike recalibrates the rate. Whether more, I suppose your question is whether more is required or not required, that is a call that will be taken. As we have said, going forward, it will be up to the MPC to take a view on how it looks forward.

But obviously, we have clarified by changing the stance that there is no rate cut in the near term. What we are contemplating is either a pause or a rate hike. How deep the rate hike or shallow the rate hike will be, will depend on the evolving macroeconomic conditions and the growth-inflation dynamics.

Referring to headline alone, as we have been mentioning, while headline is our target as given to us by the Government, and we continue to focus on trying to bring headline to the target of 4%, but that is not the only thing to be seen. As we have said, the underlying inflation, the path where it is going, because especially in these times when a lot of the increase in headline inflation is because of, one, base effect, and other supply-side factors. So, headline alone may not be the right measure, and so we have to look at other measures which we have given, including core, diffusion indices, etc., so as to be able to get a view, so as to be able to infer as to what the underlying inflation is and where it is moving to.

Brij Raj:
Thank you, Sir. Sir, we will take some more questions from our left side before we come to this side. I will now request Manojit Saha from Business Standard to ask his question. Manojit, please.

Manojit Saha, Business Standard:
Thank you, sir. Credit growth has been very strong. It's almost 19% rate. With this rate hike and, of course, as you said that going ahead, there will be no rate cut, either it will be a pause or rate hike, so interest rates will harden overall, generally. Do you expect credit growth to kind of taper down, slow down a bit from here? And if you can also tell us about your assessment of the liquidity condition because core liquidity is still ₹10 trillion, I think.

Sanjay Malhotra:
I will answer one question.

Manojit Saha:
Okay.

Sanjay Malhotra:
And I will answer your second question in case others do not ask the same question. I am sure it will come up. Your first question on credit growth - as I mentioned even earlier, in the last press conference, it has been at all-time highs, I think, in the past, the data that we have, 19% growth rate is amongst the highest. And it is because of a number of reasons. Will it moderate going forward? I think it will continue to be strong. A few percentage points here and there should not really matter too much in the overall scheme of things, but it will continue to support. It will be strong and continue to support growth.

Manojit Saha:
Thank you.

Brij Raj:
Thank you, Sir. I will request Anup Roy from Bloomberg to ask his question. Anup, please.

Anup Roy, Bloomberg:
Thank you, sir. Sir, you mentioned about the global factors today in your statement. Now, how much the global factors like US Fed policy, etc., are weighing on RBI policy decision now? Or is it still very much focused on domestic factors?

Sanjay Malhotra:
No, primarily, our policy decisions are based on the domestic growth and inflation and macroeconomic conditions and outlook. But this does not certainly mean that external forces, conditions, do not matter. They do matter. They do impact our growth, inflation, and our interest rates, as I mentioned in an earlier interview. And they are discussed, as has also been noted in the minutes, always. So, they are taken into consideration in our monetary policy decisions.

Brij Raj:
Thank you, Sir. I will request Hamsini Karthik from Moneycontrol to ask her question. Hamsini, please.

Hamsini Karthik, Moneycontrol:
Thank you. Good afternoon, everyone. Sir, my question is about the liquidity available in the system at the moment. Every time there has been a flush of liquidity in the system, NBFCs have been the biggest beneficiaries of credit. What this has invariably led to is a little bit of an asset quality issue. Now on one side, RBI is trying to restrict revolving credit as a product, and there is also drought situation emerging in some of the critical credit pockets as well. How do you see the scenario play out, the scenario of high liquidity plus revolving credit getting tapered? Are you confident that we are not going to have a similar situation of asset quality issues?

Sanjay Malhotra:
Yes, I mean NBFC growth rate has been quite robust, about 37% credit growth by banks to NBFCs, and NBFC credit growth itself is also quite robust. Overall, I think it is lower than that of banks. We will have to check, but I think it is less. NBFC credit to the real economy is lower than that of the banks.

We do not see any issues or concerns relating to asset quality with regard to NBFCs. We are always alert to such risks getting developed, not only from an asset quality point of view, but as noted by the MPC, also on demand and price pressures getting built. So we are conscious of such risks, but we do not see any such risks getting built as of now.

Hamsini Karthik:
Thank you.

Brij Raj:
Thank you, Sir. I will request Ekta Suri from Zee Business to ask her question. Ekta, please.

Ekta Suri, Zee Business:
Good afternoon, sir. Sir, my question is a slight follow-up on Hamsini's question. If there is no asset quality issue in NBFCs, then regarding the demand for revolving credit they argue that they reach the last mile, could some relaxation be given alongside term loans? Or is the RBI essentially telling NBFCs that this is not the rule, why did you start it, and whether the draft directions were meant to remind them of that?

Sanjay Malhotra:
You asked the question and gave the answer as well. Primarily, as you said, the draft regulations we published are, in a way, a clarification. It is not a new rule or regulation because NBFCs were not permitted to offer revolving credit. This is not merely a clarification; directions in this regard were given multiple times to individual NBFCs during the RBI's supervision.

Now, due to technological advancements, by using software and technology, revolving credit is being provided in the form of a term loan. Therefore, to incorporate this into the regulations, we have published the draft directions. We have received several comments regarding this, which we are reviewing.

Whereas accommodation will mean a loose monetary policy where interest rates are low, liquidity, etc., is accordingly high, so that it spurs economic activity. And neutral means neither. In our context, we have used this more for policy guidance going forward, not so much for whether the policy itself is accommodative or whether it is restrictive. We are using it as a signal for our rates, for our policy action going forward. We use this word calibrated. Calibrated, means, that it's a milder form. All these risks are material. I think, for us as central bankers, the most significant of these is cyber risks. Already in this day and age, when IT is being used by all systems and when there are no borders between the financial systems and they interact with each other, AI adds another dimension to it, and so we have to be very vigilant with regard to these. We are already taking a number of measures through our regulation and supervision departments, and we are fortifying our systems so that we are able to mitigate and prevent cyber risks from emerging.

Brij Raj:
Thank you, Sir. I will request Prarthana from Akashvani to ask her question. Prarthana, please.

C. Prarthana, Akashvani:
Good afternoon, Governor. The RBI statement released today mentions constitution of a Technical Consultative Committee for Financial Markets. Could you please elaborate on that?

Sanjay Malhotra:
Rohit [DG(RJ)], would you like to take it? It's your subject.

Rohit Jain:
So, as we have seen, the financial markets have been widening, deepening, a lot of reforms have been done, and we are taking various regulatory measures to further strengthen the markets and also develop the markets further.

So, we were already doing a lot of engagement with market participants, a lot of dialogue happens, but we thought that, in view of the extreme volatility that we are seeing globally and the need to have expert views in a structured way, we are institutionalizing this arrangement where we will constitute a technical committee of expert.

And we will meet them at periodic intervals to take their inputs, their suggestions, with the whole idea that we will be able to improve policy making and also the operational issues that financial markets face. We will be able to get better understanding and information relating to this and it will help the overall cause of developing our financial markets to serve our needs.

Brij Raj:
Thank you, Sirs. We now come to the last media person. I will request Soumyajit Saha from Nikkei to ask his question. Soumyajit, please.

Soumyajit Saha, Nikkei:
Thank you, Governor. I don't have a question - a specific question, but I just want to understand what the oil price assumption is in-house, if it has changed from August, and if it has changed, what the reasoning is behind your change in those assumptions.

Sanjay Malhotra:
Would you like to answer this? [DG (PG)]

Dr. Poonam Gupta:
Sure. Oil price assumptions are given in the MPR, which has been released this time along with policy. It has increased by US$5 a barrel, and the reason is re-escalation of the conflict, prices remaining high, and the forward markets predicting that the prices would be higher than was seen in the last couple of policies. So, taken together, it is an increase, but it's, quantitatively, not a very large increase. As you know, the situation is evolving, and this is our best estimate at this time of how the annual average will turn out to be.

Sanjay Malhotra:
US$95?

Dr. Poonam Gupta:
US$95, yes.

Brij Raj:
Thank you, Sir, and thank you, Madam. Sir, with your permission, we will now conclude this press conference.

Latha Venkatesh, CNBC TV18:
Just one more, Sir. Rupee has fallen ₹50 paise today, Sir. It is very close to the all-time low of ₹96.96. We're at ₹96.83. Is there any reaction, any further steps? Should we be worried?

Sanjay Malhotra:
As I mentioned to you, we will ensure that the rupee stabilizes, that the rupee finds its correct value, and we will support the rupee in an orderly movement of the rupee and in finding its correct value, and at the same time, in ensuring that there is no excessive volatility.

Anurag Shah, ET Now Swadesh:
Sir, there were 24 questions in English and only 02 in Hindi. And Sir, there was a very big announcement...

Sanjay Malhotra:
You are only two people, so there are two.

Anurag Shah:
Sir, but the country's population is 100 crores. Sir, it was a very big announcement. A big announcement related to common people was made, and no one asked a question about it, Sir. It was related to Account Aggregator...

Sanjay Malhotra:
Thank you very much, otherwise. I was going to mention this myself.

Anurag Shah:
Sir, so the question is related to that, and...

Sanjay Malhotra:
Since you have asked, that's good. Please ask.

Anurag Shah:
Sir, to provide some context so that people understand the benefit. Sir, in May-June, a draft was issued by you regarding financial products sold through banking services, which also includes insurance, and taking that forward, IRDAI also issued a discussion paper where at the end, it is the people who will benefit, the banking customers will benefit. And Sir, this Account Aggregator, how big of a development is this, and for the common people, for the rural...

Sanjay Malhotra:
I wanted to explain this. For everyone's convenience, you didn't ask about the Account Aggregator earlier, but you asked at the end, so thank you that you paid attention to it. Yes?

Anurag Shah:
Yes, Sir, about the Account Aggregator...

Sanjay Malhotra:
So, Account Aggregator is an important means, and I would like all of you to kindly publicize this, because it is of use not only for the economy, even for you as individuals, because it gives you an overview of all your financial assets.

And so, this is now a step to integrate the information that could have been got through a number of account aggregators. There are, I think, at least 15 or so of these account aggregators, so the information was quite disaggregated. And by integrating them, now it is possible for you as individuals, as well as for other users - could be insurance brokers, could be asset managers, and investment advisors, etc., to take data with consent, with consent of the individual concerned, and appropriately advise all of us.

So, this is one, and the other is, some of you would be getting a CAS, a Consolidated Account Statement. It does not have information on bank deposits, which is a missing piece. So, we are now trying to facilitate that information relating to bank deposits across all banks, whichsoever are already onboarded, and rest will be over a period of time, with anyone account aggregator to get available to you through CAS. Thank you very much.

Hamsini Karthik:
Why are you doing this, Sir? What is the logic of including bank deposits in CAS?

Sanjay Malhotra:
Would you not like to have that information? I mean, I would like to have it i.e., my consolidated account statement. And so, at a glance, every month, if I get that information, that is I think, empowering the consumers. We see a lot of banks, a lot of cases of, what do you say, these bank deposits getting lost, and especially when people die, etc. And so, it will also help in that, because you have one view of all your financial assets.

Ekta Suri:
Sir, the regulator also issued a direction - the suggestion they gave on how to stop money going into mule accounts so that people get their money back - you issued a draft stating that the money should be blocked, and if the account is very suspicious, it becomes a mule account. So, Sir, in the public interest, we would like to know, how quickly should someone report this, and if money has gone into an account and it has already been withdrawn, cannot be blocked, what should the victim do in that case?

Sanjay Malhotra:
An SOP has already been issued for that, and under that SOP, the sooner you inform, the faster the information will reach the banks, allowing the account or the amount, whatever it is, to be frozen and returned to the owner. So, it should be done as quickly as possible. Thank you.

Brij Raj:
Thank you Sir. Thank you all for your participation, and a good day ahead.

item.title: Preserving Financial Stability in an Evolving World - Special Address by Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank of India, at the Fifth Kautilya Economic Conclave on October 3, 2026 -
item.description:
Thank you for inviting me to speak today.

2. I would like to speak on financial stability, the institutional mechanism, approach and tools for financial stability in our country, the emerging global risks, and our assessment of the financial system.

I. What is Financial Stability?

3. As we all know, financial stability is the ability of the financial system to facilitate and enhance economic and financial transactions, manage risks, and absorb shocks1. A stable financial system is one in which financial intermediaries, markets and market infrastructures reliably provide the financial services that households and businesses depend on, including during periods of economic and financial market stress. It is a system in which households and businesses have the ability and confidence to save, borrow, invest, insure, make payments, manage risk and plan for the future2.

II. Why financial stability?

4. One may ask the question: why talk about financial stability when the global financial system, despite repeated shocks, has been rather resilient and financial markets orderly. India too has had a stable financial system and among the strongest balance-sheets – of banks, corporates, governments and households – for a long period of time.

5. In fact, it is these very prolonged periods of stability that can encourage risk-taking and leverage, while fading memories of past crises can weaken the appetite for prudence, as Minsky's Financial Instability Hypothesis3 reminds us.

6. I say this not because we see signs of any imminent stress but because we need to remind ourselves to remain alert to the risks. Our experience of the past two decades offers an important lesson: banking stress can build quickly and take years to resolve. It took nearly a decade to clean up the legacy of excessive lending and NPAs from the early 2000s. We cannot afford to become complacent; the economic and financial costs of allowing vulnerabilities to build up are simply too high.

7. There is another reason why I wish to speak on this topic. The international order that emerged in the aftermath of the Washington Consensus, providing the broad framework for decades of globalisation, economic integration and relative stability, is under considerable strain. Geopolitical and geo-economic fragmentation, strategic realignment, trade restrictions, repeated supply shocks, technological disruption and climate-related risks are interacting in ways that are difficult to predict, and even more difficult to model using historical relationships. For central banks, this has important implications, as we cannot look at price and financial stability in isolation from these developments.

III. Financial Stability in India – the Institutional Mechanism

8. In the Indian context, while the RBI Act, 1934 does not explicitly mandate RBI to maintain financial stability, it is implicit in the various functions allocated to it. Let me describe a few. The preamble to the RBI Act assigns RBI the responsibility to maintain monetary stability and price stability.4 Section 45W of the same Act requires RBI to regulate the financial system of the country to its advantage. FEMA, 1999 provides for the orderly development and maintenance of the forex market.

9. It is also germane to mention that the mandate of price stability cannot be achieved without financial stability. A stable financial system is essential for the effective transmission of monetary policy. Similarly, the full potential of economic growth can only be realised if the financial system is healthy and stable.

10. Being the regulator and supervisor of banks, NBFCs and payment systems, the lender of last resort and deposit insurer gives the RBI the mandate, capability and the tools to assess emerging vulnerabilities and take timely corrective action.

11. The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) and its sub-committee provide the institutional mechanism to exchange information and coordinate policy actions with other financial sector regulators and the government agencies to preserve financial system stability.

IV. Financial Stability in India – Approach and the Tools

12. As for our approach to preserving financial stability, we realise that we cannot prevent every shock, whether originating in the real economy, or through a geopolitical event, commodity price shock or technological disruption. What we can ensure is that the financial system acts as a shock absorber. Our focus therefore is on enhancing the resilience of the financial system.

13. We achieve this through a combination of tools - prudent regulation, risk-based supervision, macroprudential measures, liquidity support including emergency liquidity assistance and resolution.

14. Our regulations focus on building a financial system that is well-capitalised, liquid and well-governed so as to enable it to manage and absorb shocks. We recognise that attempting to remove all risks would curtail innovation and investment. Regulations, therefore, strive to strike the right balance between risk management and supporting economic growth.

15. We have a well-developed system of off-site and on-site supervision. Our supervisory approach increasingly draws on data analytics, technology-enabled surveillance and thematic assessments to identify emerging risks and vulnerabilities at an early stage. We periodically conduct stress tests to identify vulnerabilities and check resilience. In collaboration with the other financial sector regulators, we present our assessment of financial stability in the half-yearly Financial Stability Reports (FSR).
